explanations.explanation: That's the plan, baker. The chief priests and scribes want Jesus arrested and killed, and they want it done on the quiet (Mark 14:1). Covert means hidden, like trying to swipe a cookie off the cooling rack while the whole family stands right there. It never works, but they're sure it will.

explanations.answer: Question Jesus in front of a crowd
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Mark 14:1 says they're looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him. Then they say, “But not during the feast… or there may be a riot among the people.” (Mark 14:2) A riot is what they're worried about, and that's like hiding a batch of cookies on a table in the middle of the room.

Close, but they're after much more than a move across town. Mark 14:1 says they're looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him. Nobody's talking about a goodbye party and a ride to the city gate. It's a heavy plan, so I'll just say that plainly.

Yep, a riot. The chief priests and scribes say, “But not during the feast, or there may be a riot among the people.” (Mark 14:2) So their plan has a calendar problem. They're sneaky, but they still have to wait for the right time, like me waiting on the timer to ding before I open the oven.

A famine is a lack of food, baker, and a feast is the opposite. Mark 14:2 has them saying, “or there may be a riot among the people.” They're worried about a crowd that gets stirred up, not an empty pantry. Honestly, an empty cookie jar can stir up a crowd too, but that's a different story.

I see where the head went, but no plague in this one. The leaders say, “But not during the feast, or there may be a riot among the people.” (Mark 14:2) Their worry is the people themselves, and what the crowd might do. A big crowd at a feast is a lot of folks in one place, and they know it.

explanations.answer: Breaks it open and pours it on Jesus' head
explanations.explanation: That's exactly it. She broke open the jar and poured the perfume on Jesus' head (Mark 14:3). Once a jar is broken open, there's no closing it back up. It's like me tipping a whole jar of sprinkles over a batch, friend, because there's no scooping them back.

explanations.answer: Hands it to Simon as a gift for the house
explanations.explanation: Nope, no gift for the house. Mark 14:3 says the woman broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus' head. Simon the Leper's home is the place where it happens. Jesus' head is where the perfume goes.

explanations.answer: Sets it down unopened at Jesus' feet
explanations.explanation: Close on the setting, since it all happens in Simon the Leper's home. But Mark 14:3 says she broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus' head. So the jar was opened, not left sitting there unopened. And the perfume went on His head.

That's the number, baker. The grumblers say it could have been sold for “…over three hundred denarii…” (Mark 14:5). A denarius is a coin, and three hundred of them is a big pile. I'd be checking my apron pockets for loose change just hearing that.

Good guess pulling a number, but it isn't the one here. At this table, the grumblers say the perfume could have been sold for “…over three hundred denarii…” (Mark 14:5). A denarius is a coin, and they're figuring the price out fast.

Good try pulling out a number, but this one isn't from this table. The grumblers say the perfume could have been sold for “…over three hundred denarii…” (Mark 14:5). A denarius is a coin, and they're counting up the price like they already have a calculator out.

Right on the money, baker. The grumblers say it could have been sold “…and the money given to the poor.” (Mark 14:5) Helping the poor is a good thing, and Jesus says so Himself in verse 7. Still, they scolded the woman over it, and that's where their talk went sideways.

Not the priests, friend. The grumblers say the perfume could have been sold “…and the money given to the poor.” (Mark 14:5) The chief priests show up in verses 1 and 10 of this passage, but the grumblers' words here are about the poor.

Good guess, but the temple isn't mentioned at this dinner. The grumblers say the money could have been “…given to the poor.” (Mark 14:5) The perfume was poured out in a home in Bethany, so a donation box didn't come into it.

explanations.answer: Anointed His body in advance of His burial
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says, baker. “She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.” (Mark 14:8) She poured out the perfume, and Jesus told them what it meant. Burial is the word He uses.

explanations.answer: Marked Him as the king who was coming
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but that's not what Jesus says in this passage. He says, “She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.” (Mark 14:8) The word He uses is burial. Sometimes the answer is quieter than the one we expected, friend.

explanations.answer: Made Him ready for the Passover meal
explanations.explanation: The Passover was two days away, so I see the connection. But Jesus says something else. “She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.” (Mark 14:8) He points ahead to His burial, not to a dinner plate.

explanations.answer: It will be told in memory of her
explanations.explanation: Yes, ma'am, yes, sir. Jesus says, “And truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” (Mark 14:9) I want my cookies remembered, and she gets the whole world. That's a lot of retelling, baker.

explanations.answer: It will be kept quiet among the Twelve
explanations.explanation: Quiet is the opposite of what Jesus says. “…wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” (Mark 14:9) The Twelve are the group Judas belongs to (Mark 14:10), and this promise reaches way past them. It goes to all the world, friend.

explanations.answer: It will be written on the temple wall
explanations.explanation: Nice picture, but Jesus doesn't say anything about a wall. He says, “…what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” (Mark 14:9) The promise reaches wherever the gospel is preached in all the world. That's a lot farther than one temple, baker.

That's him, baker. Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus (Mark 14:10). This is one of the heavy parts of the story, so I'll just say that plainly. I think it's a hard line to read.

Thaddaeus is one of the Twelve too, but he's not the one in this verse (Mark 3:18). Mark 14:10 says it was Judas Iscariot who went to the chief priests to betray Jesus. It's a heavy moment, friend, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

Bartholomew is one of the Twelve as well, but he's not the one here (Mark 3:18). Mark 14:10 says Judas Iscariot went to the chief priests to betray Jesus. This part of the story is a heavy one, baker.

That's the word, baker. “They were delighted to hear this, and they promised to give him money.” (Mark 14:11) The chief priests had been searching for a covert way, and then one of the Twelve walked right up to them. I think that's a hard thing to read, so I'll say it plainly.
Yep, money, friend. The chief priests “…promised to give him money.” (Mark 14:11) The text names money and stops there. It doesn't give a number in this passage, so I'm not going to make one up.

Not troubled. Mark 14:11 says, “They were delighted to hear this…” They had been looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus, and Judas came to them. I think this is one of the heavy spots in the story, baker.
No land in this one, friend. The verse says they “…promised to give him money.” (Mark 14:11) Land isn't what the verse names. I think it's a sad one to read.
Not power, baker. Mark 14:11 says the chief priests “…promised to give him money.” Power isn't what the verse names. I think it's a heavy part of the story.
